meta.blurb: Illustrator Lena has aching eyes at night, and her son Milo squints at the school board. A friendly optometrist shows them how eyes really work, what screens do and do not do, and which habits, from daylight to slow blinks, can help.
meta.bible: Lena Hart: an illustrator who works from home at two screens, tired and worried, practical and curious. Milo: her son, nine years old, who loves cameras and football and gets round blue glasses. Omar: Milo's father, short-sighted since he was twelve. Dina: Lena's sister, who wears contact lenses. Lena's mother: needs reading glasses. Mr Farouk: a gentle optometrist at a small shop called Clear Sight on the high street, who explains in plain words, says what science does not know, and gives only general information. The story runs from one Saturday eye test to a check-up six months later. Key terms: Cornea, Pupil, Iris, Lens, Retina, Rods, Cones, Optic nerve, Optometrist, Myopia, Short-sightedness, Long-sightedness, Astigmatism, Presbyopia, Digital eye strain, Tear film, Blink, Glare, Ultraviolet, Glaucoma, Diabetes, Floaters, Detached retina, Contact lenses, Vitamin A, World Health Organization. Facts used, all general and hedged: myopia usually comes from an eyeball slightly too long; genes matter; school trials in Asia that added about forty minutes to two hours of outdoor time found fewer children developed myopia, though reasons are debated; people blink much less at screens; the 20-20-20 habit has modest evidence; careful reviews found no clear benefit of blue-light glasses for eye strain; screens are not known to cause lasting damage in healthy adult eyes; the World Health Organization advises no screen time under one year and no more than an hour for ages two to four; reading in dim light and sitting close to the television are myths. Voice: calm, kind, plain and a little humorous; honest about what is not known; no diagnosis or personal medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: Lena is an illustrator who works at a computer from morning until evening. By six o'clock her eyes are burning, her head is aching and she cannot read the words on the screen.
Lena's nine-year-old son Milo comes home with a letter from school. His teacher says that he squints at the board and sometimes copies the wrong words.
Lena decides not to guess what is wrong and books an eye test for each of them. The local optician, Mr Farouk, has two free places on Saturday morning.

Mr Farouk is an optometrist, which means that he is trained to test eyes and to spot problems. He tells them that he will explain everything in plain words, but that his answers are general, and each person's eyes are different.
Mr Farouk shows Milo a large model of an eye and says that it works a bit like a camera. Light first passes through the cornea, which is the clear window at the front.

The small black circle is called the pupil, and the coloured ring around it is the iris. The iris makes the pupil larger in the dark and smaller in bright light, and behind it sits the lens, which focuses the light.
At the back of the eye lies the retina, a thin layer that senses light. It contains millions of cells called rods and cones, and they turn light into tiny electrical signals.
The signals leave the eye along the optic nerve, which is a thick cable of nerve fibres. The brain does the final work, turning the signals into the picture that we think of as seeing.

To look at something close, a tiny muscle inside the eye squeezes the lens into a rounder shape. Like any muscle, it can tire after hours of close work, which is one reason why reading and screens make the eyes ache.
The front of the eye is covered by a thin film of tears. Each time you blink, your eyelid spreads fresh tears over the surface, which keeps it moist, smooth and clean.
Milo reads the letters on the chart with each eye, and the bottom lines are blurred. Mr Farouk tells Lena that Milo is short-sighted, and that her own eyes are healthy but a little tired.
Short-sightedness, also called myopia, makes close things clear and faraway things blurry. It usually happens because the eyeball is slightly too long, so light focuses just in front of the retina.

Mr Farouk lists the other common problems with sight. Long-sightedness makes near things hard to see, astigmatism makes things look slightly stretched, and presbyopia is the loss of near focus that comes with age.
Lena asks the question that has been troubling her: did screens cause Milo's short-sightedness? Mr Farouk answers honestly that science does not yet give a simple yes or no.

Family history matters a great deal when it comes to eyes, Mr Farouk says. He asks whether either parent is short-sighted, and Lena says that Milo's father, Omar, has worn thick glasses since he was twelve.

Some school trials have found that children who spend more time outdoors in daylight are less likely to become short-sighted. Scientists are still working out why, and bright light may be part of the answer.
Milo chooses a pair of round blue glasses and puts them on. Mr Farouk explains that wearing glasses does not make eyes weaker, and that Milo should wear them whenever he needs to see clearly.

Mr Farouk explains that some children with fast-changing eyesight are offered treatments to slow it down. These include special lenses or drops, but they are decided on by a specialist, and they are not right for everybody.
That evening Lena turns to her own problem, because her eyes still ache. She asks Mr Farouk what happens to the eyes during a long day at a screen.

After long periods at a screen, many people notice tired, dry or blurry eyes, headaches, and a stiff neck or shoulders. Doctors call this digital eye strain, and the symptoms usually go away after a rest.
When we concentrate on a screen, we blink much less often than usual. The tears on the surface of the eye then dry out faster, and that makes the eyes feel gritty and sore.
Mr Farouk shows Lena how to blink slowly and fully, closing her eyelids all the way. He suggests that she does this several times whenever she stops to think, so that the tears spread again.
Mr Farouk describes a popular habit called the twenty-twenty-twenty rule. Every twenty minutes, look at something about twenty feet, or six metres, away for twenty seconds.
Mr Farouk advises sitting about an arm's length from the screen, with the top of it a little below eye level. Looking slightly down is easier on both the eyes and the neck.

Glare from a window or a lamp can make the eyes work harder. Mr Farouk suggests setting the screen's brightness to match the room, and placing the screen so that bright light does not shine straight on it.
Small text makes people lean forward and squint, which tires the eyes. Mr Farouk suggests making the text larger and keeping a clear contrast between the words and the background.
Lena asks about glasses that filter blue light, which are advertised for screen users. Mr Farouk says that careful reviews of the research have not found that they reduce eye strain.

Lena asks whether screens will damage her eyes for ever, because that is her biggest fear. As far as researchers know, the strain is temporary, and screens have not been shown to cause lasting damage in healthy adult eyes.
Heaters and air conditioning dry the air, and dry air can make dry eyes feel worse. If the dryness continues, Mr Farouk suggests asking a pharmacist or an optometrist about eye drops.
When she gets home, Lena moves her desk sideways to the window and raises her screen on a box. She sets a reminder to stand up and look at the garden every twenty minutes.
Mr Farouk mentions that screens can also affect sleep. Bright light late in the evening can delay sleep for some people, so many experts suggest switching screens off about an hour before bed.
During sleep the eyes are closed and they rest from the work of focusing. Mr Farouk says that people who sleep well tend to find that their eyes feel more comfortable the next day.
The World Health Organization advises no screen time for babies under one year old. It suggests no more than one hour a day for children aged two to four, and less is better.
Lena, Omar and Milo agree on a plan for screens at home. Milo will take breaks, play outside every day, and keep meals free of screens, and the adults will follow the same rules.
Many people believe that reading in dim light ruins the eyes. In fact, it can make the eyes tired, but there is no good evidence that it causes lasting damage.

Another myth says that sitting close to the television harms the eyes, and Mr Farouk says that it does not. A child who always sits very close, however, might not see well from further away, so an eye test is a good idea.
The body needs vitamin A to see, and carrots contain it, but eating extra carrots will not give anyone better sight. A balanced diet is good for the whole body, including the eyes.

Strong sunlight contains ultraviolet light, which can harm the eyes over many years. Mr Farouk recommends sunglasses that block ultraviolet light, and a hat, and he warns people never to look straight at the sun.
Many of the serious eye injuries that doctors see are easy to prevent. Safety goggles protect the eyes when people drill, saw, trim hedges or play sports where a ball or an elbow can reach the face.

Lena's sister Dina wears contact lenses, so Mr Farouk gives some general advice. She should wash her hands first, follow the cleaning instructions, and never sleep in her lenses unless her optometrist says that it is safe.

Some eye problems are real emergencies, and Mr Farouk lists them. Sudden loss of vision, a dark curtain across the sight, many new floaters or flashes, or severe pain all need urgent help from a doctor.
Some serious eye diseases, such as glaucoma, can develop slowly without any early symptoms. People with diabetes are also at risk, so regular eye tests are important for them.
Over lunch, Lena's mother holds the menu at arm's length and complains that the print is tiny. Mr Farouk had explained that this is normal, because the lens in the eye grows stiffer with age.
How often someone needs an eye test depends on their age, their eyes and their health. Mr Farouk says that for most adults every two years is common, but it is best to ask your own optometrist.

Children often do not realise that they cannot see well, because their vision has always been like that. Squinting, holding things close, rubbing the eyes or complaining of headaches are good reasons for an eye test.
A month later, Lena's headaches are far less frequent. Her eyes feel fresher in the evenings, and she is still using the twenty-minute breaks that Mr Farouk suggested.
Milo plays outside after school every day, and at weekends the whole family goes to the park. He wears his blue glasses, and he has stopped squinting at the board in class.
Six months later, Milo returns for another test, and his eyes have changed only a little. Mr Farouk tells the family that they will keep checking him, because children's eyes can change quickly.
Mr Farouk sums up what the family has learned. Daylight, breaks, good posture and regular tests help, and science is still learning about screens, so he tells them to be curious and not afraid.
This book has given general information about eyes, screens and rest, and research is still growing. It is not medical advice, so please see an optometrist or a doctor about your own eyes.
C1C2: Lena, an illustrator who worked from home, had spent nine hours bent over two glowing screens, and by six o'clock the words on them had begun to swim. Her eyes burned, a dull ache sat behind her forehead, and the lamp beside her seemed suddenly too bright. She closed the laptop, rubbed her eyelids gently and wondered whether her work was slowly ruining her sight.

Her nine-year-old son Milo arrived home that evening with a letter from his teacher, who had noticed that he squinted at the board and sometimes copied the wrong words into his book. Lena realised that he had also been creeping closer to the television for months, and that she had put it down to an ordinary childhood habit. A cold worry settled in her stomach, because both of them now seemed to have trouble with their eyes.

Lena decided that guessing was no use and that the sensible thing to do was to ask a professional, so she booked an eye test for each of them. The little optician's shop on the high street, called Clear Sight, had two free places on Saturday morning, with a man named Mr Farouk. She wrote the time on the calendar in large letters, and felt better for having made a plan.

Mr Farouk was a tall, gentle man in a white coat, who introduced himself as an optometrist, a professional trained to test sight, prescribe glasses and notice signs of eye disease. He promised to explain everything in plain words while Milo waited, but he warned that what he said in general would not replace an examination of their own eyes. Lena found that the warning, oddly, made her trust him a great deal more.

To pass the time before the test, Mr Farouk placed a large model of an eye in front of Milo and explained that it works rather like a camera. Light from the world first passes through the cornea, the clear dome at the front, which does most of the bending of the light, and then enters through a small opening. Milo, who loved cameras more than almost anything, leaned forward with a sudden burst of interest.

The small black circle in the middle of the eye is the pupil, Mr Farouk said, and the coloured ring around it, the iris, is a muscle that makes the pupil wider in dim light and narrower in bright light. Behind the iris sits the lens, a clear, flexible disc that fine-tunes the focus and lets the eye see clearly at different distances. Milo shone a small torch at his own eye in the mirror and watched his pupil shrink.

The light travels on through the clear jelly inside the eyeball until it lands on the retina, a delicate layer at the back that works like the sensor of a camera. It contains millions of specialised cells, the rods that cope with dim light and the cones that detect colour and fine detail, and these turn the light into tiny electrical signals. Milo was impressed to learn that the picture on the retina is actually upside down.

From the retina, Mr Farouk continued, the signals travel along the optic nerve, a cable made of about a million fine fibres, to the back of the brain. It is the brain, not the eye, that turns those signals into a picture, turns the upside-down image the right way up and adds meaning, so that seeing is really a partnership between the two. Lena had never thought of her eyes as part of her brain, and she found the idea oddly moving.

When we look at something close, Mr Farouk said, a tiny ring of muscle inside the eye tightens and lets the lens become rounder, which brings near objects into focus. Looking at faraway things relaxes the muscle, so hours of close work keep it working steadily, rather like holding a small weight at arm's length. That is one reason why a long day of reading or screen work leaves the eyes feeling tired, he added, although it is not the only one.

The front surface of the eye, Mr Farouk went on, is protected by a thin film of tears made of water, oils and mucus, and every blink spreads it fresh across the surface like a windscreen wiper. A smooth, moist film is essential for clear vision as well as comfort, and when it breaks up the eyes sting, water and blur. Lena realised with a start that she could not remember the last time she had blinked properly at her desk.

Milo covered one eye, then the other, and read the letters on the chart as far down as he could, until the bottom lines dissolved into a grey blur. Mr Farouk, after a careful examination, told Lena that Milo was short-sighted, a very common condition that glasses can correct, and that her own eyes were healthy though they showed signs of strain. For the first time that week Lena was able to breathe out, and she squeezed Milo's shoulder.

Short-sightedness, which doctors call myopia, means that nearby things look sharp while distant ones look blurred, Mr Farouk explained, and it usually arises when the eyeball grows slightly too long. Light then comes to a focus just in front of the retina instead of exactly on it, so that the picture is out of focus by the time it arrives. A pair of glasses simply bends the light a little before it enters the eye, he said, and puts the focus back where it belongs.

Short-sightedness has relatives, Mr Farouk said, and he listed them like members of a family. Long-sightedness makes near objects difficult to see, astigmatism, which comes from an eye that is not perfectly round, makes things look slightly stretched or blurred, while presbyopia is the slow stiffening of the lens in middle age. All of them can usually be corrected, he reassured her, with glasses, contact lenses or sometimes surgery.

At last Lena asked the question that had been troubling her all week, which was whether all the time Milo had spent on tablets and games had damaged his eyes. Mr Farouk answered honestly that the science does not offer a simple yes or no, because short-sightedness has become much more common around the world and several things seem to play a part. Screens may be one of them, he said, but nobody has proved that they are the main cause, and she should not blame herself.

One of the strongest clues, Mr Farouk said, is family history, because children with one short-sighted parent are more likely to become short-sighted, and those with two are more likely still. Lena nodded slowly, remembering that Omar had worn thick glasses since he was twelve years old and had sometimes joked that he could not find his own shoes without them. Genes, it seemed, may have written part of Milo's story long before any tablet arrived.

One of the most encouraging findings, Mr Farouk said, comes from school trials in Asia in which children spent between about forty minutes and two hours more outdoors each school day, and fewer of them went on to develop short-sightedness. Scientists are still debating the reason, though many suspect that the brightness of daylight plays a part, and the effect appears to work best in preventing myopia before it starts. It is no guarantee for any one child, he added, but it is cheap, pleasant and healthy for many other reasons.

Milo tried on a dozen pairs before choosing a round blue frame, and when he put them on he turned to the window and gasped at the sudden sharpness of the trees across the road. A common worry, Mr Farouk said, is that wearing glasses makes the eyes lazy or weaker, but there is no good evidence for that, and a child who sees clearly is simply better able to learn and to play. Lena felt a rush of relief and a small unexpected pang, because her little boy looked suddenly older.

In some children, Mr Farouk said, short-sightedness keeps increasing year after year, and for them specialists sometimes recommend treatments that can slow its progress, such as specially designed lenses and, in some countries, low-dose eye drops. Each has benefits and drawbacks, he warned, and the choice has to be made after a full examination by a trained professional, so he would not recommend anything for Milo yet. He would check Milo again in six months, he told Lena, and let her know if anything had changed.

Once Milo had gone to play with his new glasses, Lena turned the conversation to her own sore eyes, which had been troubling her for months. She asked Mr Farouk what actually happens inside the eyes during a long day at a screen, and whether she should worry that she was doing permanent harm. He pulled up a stool and told her that this was one of the commonest complaints he heard from people who worked at computers.

The symptoms Lena described, Mr Farouk said, are so common that they have a name of their own, digital eye strain, and they include tired, dry or blurred eyes, headaches and an aching neck after long hours at a screen. It is uncomfortable and sometimes distracting, but as far as we know it is temporary, and the symptoms usually fade after a rest. He added that the same symptoms can sometimes have other causes, so anyone with persistent trouble should have an eye test.

One of the main culprits, Mr Farouk said, is the way people stare at screens, because when we concentrate hard our blinking slows down dramatically, from about fifteen times a minute to far fewer. The tear film then evaporates faster than it is replaced, and the eyes begin to feel dry, gritty and sore, rather like a windscreen without wipers on a dusty road. Many of the blinks we do make on a screen are also partial, he added, which does not spread the tears properly.

Mr Farouk showed Lena a simple exercise: close the eyelids slowly and completely, pause for a moment and then open them gently, as if she were falling asleep. He suggested that she did this a few times whenever she paused to think, so that the tears could spread across her eyes again. It sounded far too easy to matter, but Lena was willing to try anything.

Mr Farouk described a popular habit known as the twenty-twenty-twenty rule, which asks you to look at something about twenty feet, or six metres, away for twenty seconds, once every twenty minutes. The scientific evidence that it prevents eye strain is fairly modest, he admitted, but it costs nothing, does no harm and gives the focusing muscle a rest, and many people find that it helps. Lena put a small clock beside her monitor that very evening and chose the tree outside the window as her distant target.

Posture matters as well, Mr Farouk said, and a common recommendation is to sit about an arm's length from the screen, with the top of it at or just below eye level so that the gaze falls slightly downwards. Looking down lets the eyelids cover more of the eye, which reduces the surface that dries out, and it also relieves the strain in the neck that comes from craning upwards. Lena realised that her laptop had been propped on a pile of books, directly in front of her nose.

Light, Mr Farouk said, is the next thing to check, because glare from a window or a bare lamp makes the eyes struggle to see the text. A screen that is far brighter than its surroundings tires the eyes, and so does one that is much dimmer, so the brightness should roughly match the room. He suggested turning the desk sideways to the window, and Lena, glancing across the shop, noticed that his own computer stood at exactly that angle.

Tiny letters make people lean towards the screen and screw up their eyes, Mr Farouk observed, and both habits increase the strain on the eyes and neck. He recommended enlarging the text until it can be read comfortably from an arm's length, and choosing a clear contrast between the words and the background rather than a pale grey on white. Lena, who spent her days squinting at fine pencil lines, laughed with embarrassment and promised to zoom in.

Lena had seen advertisements for glasses that block the blue light from screens, and she asked whether she ought to buy a pair. Mr Farouk said that careful reviews of the research, which combine the results of many trials, have so far found no clear evidence that such lenses reduce eye strain. The habits they had discussed were likely to do more for her, he added, though some people simply like them, and nobody was being foolish for wondering.

Lena finally asked the question she had been afraid of, which was whether her screens could cause permanent harm to her eyes. As far as researchers have been able to tell, Mr Farouk replied, the discomfort caused by screens is temporary, and there is no strong evidence that they damage healthy adult eyes for good. Long-term studies are still in progress, however, and he preferred to say that we do not yet know everything rather than to pretend to a certainty that science did not yet have.

The air in many offices and homes, Mr Farouk added, is dried by heating and air conditioning, and dry air makes the tear film evaporate even faster than usual. A well-ventilated room, a little distance from the heater and enough water to drink can all help, but if the dryness persists, he said, it is worth asking a pharmacist or optometrist about suitable drops. Persistent redness or pain, though, deserves a proper examination, and should not be treated by guesswork.

Back at home, Lena wasted no time in turning her workspace into a more eye-friendly place, dragging the desk sideways to the window, raising the screen on a sturdy box and enlarging every piece of text. She set a gentle reminder on her phone to stand up every twenty minutes, look out at the garden and take a few slow blinks. Within three days, her headaches had begun to ease, though she suspected that Mr Farouk would say that three days proved very little.

On a separate visit, Mr Farouk mentioned that the effects of screens are not limited to the eyes, because bright light in the evening can delay the body clock and make it harder for some people to fall asleep. The effect varies from person to person, and warm night-time screen settings are probably of modest benefit, so many experts simply suggest switching screens off about an hour before bed. Lena, who often worked until midnight, felt a sharp twinge of guilt, and then a flicker of curiosity about how it would feel to stop.

While we sleep, Mr Farouk said, the eyes are closed and the focusing muscle finally rests, and the surface of the eye remains moist behind the eyelid. People who sleep well usually notice that their eyes feel more comfortable the next day, and those who cut their sleep short often complain of grittiness and soreness as well as tiredness. Even a minute of closing the eyes during a working day, he added, can feel surprisingly refreshing.

Turning to children, Mr Farouk said that the World Health Organization advises no screen time for babies under one, and no more than an hour a day for children aged two to four, with less being better. For older children the research is less clear, and most experts prefer sensible family rules about what, when and how long, rather than a single magic number. Lena listened carefully, and remembered how often she had handed Milo a tablet to buy herself ten quiet minutes.

That weekend, Lena, Omar and Milo drew up a family plan for screens, which Milo wrote out in his best handwriting and pinned to the fridge. It said that there would be breaks to look out of the window, an hour of outdoor play every day after school, and no screens at meals, and Milo insisted that the rules should apply to the adults as well. Omar grumbled for about a minute and then agreed, and the plan, as plans go, was working within a week.

One of the oldest warnings, Mr Farouk remarked, is that reading in dim light will ruin the eyes, and Lena admitted that her own mother had said it often. Reading in poor light does make the eyes work harder and may leave them tired, he said, but there is no good evidence that it causes lasting harm, so the belief is largely a myth. Even so, a decent lamp makes reading far more comfortable, and comfort is a perfectly good reason to switch one on.

Another familiar warning claims that sitting too close to the television will damage the eyes, and Mr Farouk smiled as he said that it is not true. The habit itself does no harm, but a child who always creeps close to the screen may be doing so because distant things look blurred, and that is a good reason to arrange an eye test. Lena thought, with a small stab of guilt, about all the times she had told Milo to move back.

Carrots, Mr Farouk said, have a reputation for improving eyesight that is rather greater than they deserve, since the vitamin A that they contain is essential for the retina but a normal, varied diet already supplies enough of it. Leafy vegetables, fish, eggs and fruit are all part of a healthy pattern of eating that is good for the eyes along with the rest of the body, but no food can cure short-sightedness. Some research looks at particular vitamins for conditions later in life, he added, and a doctor should advise on those.

Sunlight, delightful as it is, contains ultraviolet radiation that over many years can harm the surface of the eye and contribute to some conditions later in life, Mr Farouk said. He recommended sunglasses that are labelled as blocking ultraviolet light, and a hat with a brim, particularly for children, who spend long hours outdoors. He also gave a stern reminder that nobody should ever look straight at the sun, even during an eclipse, without special approved glasses.

Some of the most serious eye injuries he saw, Mr Farouk said sadly, were also the easiest to prevent, caused by flying splinters, chemicals, garden branches and sports balls. Safety goggles are a cheap and simple defence whenever someone is drilling, sawing, trimming a hedge or using strong cleaning products, and eye protection is also wise in sports where a ball or an elbow can reach the face. Omar went home and put a pair of goggles beside his toolbox that afternoon.

Lena's sister Dina wore contact lenses, so Mr Farouk was happy to give some general advice, which was to wash and dry the hands before touching the lenses and to follow the cleaning instructions exactly. People should also avoid rinsing the lenses in tap water, and should not sleep or swim in them unless their optometrist has said that it is safe, because infections of the cornea can be painful and sometimes dangerous. Lena promised to pass the whole message on to her sister over lunch on Sunday.

There are a few warning signs, Mr Farouk said gravely, that should never be left until a convenient moment. They are a sudden loss of vision, a dark curtain moving across the sight, a sudden shower of new floaters or flashes of light, and severe pain in the eye, especially with redness. These can signal conditions such as a detached retina, which need urgent attention from a doctor or an eye hospital if sight is to be saved, and Lena wrote them on a card and stuck the card to the fridge.

A particular danger, Mr Farouk explained, is that some serious eye diseases give no early warning, because the first signs are so gradual that the brain simply fills in the missing parts. Glaucoma, which damages the optic nerve, is one example, and people with diabetes are at risk of damage to the blood vessels in the retina, which is why regular eye checks are offered to them in many countries. An eye test, he said, can find such problems early, when treatment is most effective.

At lunch with her mother on Sunday, Lena watched her hold the menu at arm's length and complain that restaurants nowadays printed everything in microscopic letters. It was exactly what Mr Farouk had described, for the lens inside the eye slowly stiffens with age and finds it harder to focus on close objects, a process that affects nearly everyone from their forties or fifties. Her mother, it emerged, had not had an eye test in eleven years, and Lena gently arranged one.

Lena wanted to know how often a person ought to have an eye test, and Mr Farouk said that there is no single answer, since it depends on age, on any eye condition, on family history and on general health. For many healthy adults every two years is a common interval, children may need more frequent checks while their eyes are changing quickly, and people with conditions such as diabetes will be told to come at set times. The best advice, he said, is to ask your own optometrist, who knows your own eyes and can plan your next visit.

Children rarely complain that they cannot see, Mr Farouk said, since they have no way of knowing that the world is supposed to look sharper, and so the signs often have to be noticed by the adults around them. Squinting, tilting the head, holding books close, rubbing the eyes and complaining of headaches are all good reasons for an eye test, and a child does not need to be able to read letters for one. Lena thought of Milo's teacher, and silently thanked her for writing the letter that had started it all.

A month after the first visit, Lena noticed with quiet satisfaction that the headaches had become rare and that her eyes no longer burned by evening. She could not be sure which of the changes had made the most difference, whether the bigger text, the window, the breaks or the slow blinking, and she suspected that it was the combination that worked. What mattered, she decided, was that she could now finish the day with enough sight left to read her son a story.

Milo went outside every afternoon, his round blue glasses strapped on with a band while he played football, and on weekends the whole family spent hours in the park, enjoying the daylight and the open sky. His teacher reported that he no longer squinted at the board and that he had begun to put his hand up more often. Whether the outdoor hours would protect his eyes in the long run, nobody could say for certain, but the fresh air was doing the whole family good.

Six months later Milo returned for his check-up, and Mr Farouk reported with a smile that his eyes had changed only slightly since the last visit, and that his glasses were doing their job well. Children's eyes can change quickly, he warned, so the family would carry on with regular check-ups, and if the short-sightedness began to increase rapidly, they could talk about the options for slowing it down. Lena left the shop feeling lighter than she had in a whole year, and Milo skipped all the way to the bus stop.

Before they left, Mr Farouk summed up what the family had learned in a few plain sentences. Daylight, regular breaks, a comfortable desk and regular eye tests are all sensible and safe, he said, and the science of how screens affect the eyes, particularly those of children, is still developing. Fear is not a helpful guide, but curiosity is, and kindness to yourself, including the habit of resting your eyes and your mind, is part of eye care too.

Lena closed her laptop in the soft evening light, blinked slowly several times and looked out at the garden, where Milo was waving from the doorway in his round blue glasses. This book has offered only general information about eyes, screens and rest, and the research behind it is still growing, so it is not medical advice and cannot replace an examination by an optometrist or a doctor who knows you. If you notice any sudden change in your sight, or have any worry about your eyes, please seek professional help without delay.
